title: Who Can Make Hillel Angry?
summary: Two men made a bet of four hundred zuz: could anyone make Hillel angry? One of them came on Friday afternoon, just before Shabbat, shouting and asking strange questions again and again, but Hillel answered him every time with patience and a smile. A funny story about patience and keeping your temper.
pages: In Jerusalem long ago, everyone knew: wise Hillel never gets angry. Not when you bother him, not when you confuse him, and not when you ask him strange questions. Two men heard about this and smiled doubtfully. "There's no such thing as a person who never gets angry," said one of them.

"Let's make a bet," said the first. "If you can make Hillel angry, I'll give you four hundred zuz!" Four hundred zuz was a lot of money, almost a treasure. "I can do it," said the second man confidently. "I know exactly how."

He picked the most inconvenient time: Friday afternoon, when everyone was rushing to get ready for Shabbat. And just at that moment, Hillel was bathing and washing his hair. The man stood by the house and shouted loudly: "Who here is Hillel? Who here is Hillel?" No "hello" and no "excuse me."

Hillel heard. He didn't shout back, "What do you want now?" He wrapped himself in a robe and went out to him, still with water in his hair, and said pleasantly: "My son, what do you wish?"
"I have a question," said the man.
"Ask, my son, ask," answered Hillel.

"Why are the heads of the people of Babylon round?" asked the man. It was a silly question, and a little insulting too, because Hillel himself came from Babylon! But Hillel answered seriously: "You have asked a great question. It is because they have no skilled midwives." The man left, and Hillel went back to washing his hair.

A little while passed, and again: "Who here is Hillel? Who here is Hillel?" Once more Hillel wrapped himself up and went out. "My son, what do you wish?"
"Why are the eyes of the people of Tadmor red and teary?"
"You have asked a great question," said Hillel. "It is because they live among the sands, and the sand gets into their eyes."

The man left, and came back a third time: "Who here is Hillel? Who here is Hillel?" And again Hillel came out, just as calm as before.
"Why do people who live near swamps have wide feet?"
"Because they walk in water and mud all day, and wide feet help them not to sink," Hillel answered patiently.

The man began to sweat. Shabbat was coming, the money was in danger, and Hillel was still calm! "I have many more questions," he said, "but I'm afraid you'll get angry." Hillel sat down across from him and said: "Ask all the questions you have."

Now the man couldn't hold back anymore: "Are you Hillel? May there be no more people like you in Israel!"
"Why, my son?" asked Hillel.
"Because of you I lost four hundred zuz!"

Even now, Hillel didn't get angry. He told him: "Be careful with your temper. Hillel is worth losing four hundred zuz over, and another four hundred zuz, and still Hillel will not get angry."
In other words: watch out for your anger. Even if you lose more and more money because of me, Hillel will not get angry.

The man went home without the money, but with something else: he had seen with his own eyes that you can answer kindly, even when someone is trying to make you angry. And you? What do you do when someone bothers you again and again? Maybe next time try taking a deep breath, smiling, and asking like Hillel: "What do you wish?"
